title: Ἱκέτης Πρίαμος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Priam, still taking his guide for a follower of Achilles, asks whether his son’s body has been given to the dogs. Hermes tells him it lies unharmed by Achilles’ ship, fresh after twelve days, its wounds closed, for the gods look after Hector even in death. Priam offers the stranger a goblet, but Hermes refuses to take gifts behind Achilles’ back; he drives the wagon on, puts the camp’s sentries to sleep, opens the gate and brings Priam and the ransom to Achilles’ hut, which is described in detail. There Hermes reveals himself, tells Priam to clasp Achilles’ knees and beg him in the name of his father, mother and child, and goes back to Olympus. Priam, leaving the herald with the animals, comes in unseen, kisses Achilles’ hands, and, as Achilles and his men stare in wonder, begs him to remember his own father, tells of his fifty sons and Hector’s death, and asks for pity.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα γέρων Πρίαμος θεοειδής·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita gerōn Priamos theoeidēs·
sentences.l: Him then answered the old man Priam, godlike in form:
sentences.i: Then Priam, the old man, godlike in form, answered him:
sentences.n: This is the fixed formula for a reply: τὸν is Hermes, and δ’ marks the turn of speaker. Priam still takes his guide for a Myrmidon, one of Achilles’ men, as the stranger has told him; he does not know he is speaking to a god. ἠμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, and θεοειδής ‘godlike in form’ is Priam’s stock epithet (θεός + εἶδος ‘form’).

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν δὴ θεράπων Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος
εἴς, ἄγε δή μοι πᾶσαν ἀληθείην κατάλεξον,
ἢ ἔτι πὰρ νήεσσιν ἐμὸς πάϊς, ἦέ μιν ἤδη
ᾗσι κυσὶν μελεϊστὶ ταμὼν προύθηκεν Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.tr:
ei men dē therapōn Pēlēïadeō Achilēos
eis, age dē moi pasan alētheiēn katalexon,
ē eti par nēessin emos païs, ēe min ēdē
hēisi kysin meleïsti tamōn prouthēken Achilleus.
sentences.l:
“If you are indeed an attendant of Peleus’-son Achilles,
come, tell me all the truth,
whether my son is still by the ships, or whether now
having cut him limb by limb Achilles has set him out for his own dogs.”
sentences.i: “If you really are an attendant of Peleus’ son Achilles, come, tell me the whole truth: whether my son is still by the ships, or whether Achilles has by now cut him limb from limb and set him out for his own dogs.”
sentences.n: The speaker is Priam, and his question is about Hector’s body. εἰ μὲν δὴ … εἴς is ‘if you really are …’; εἴς is a Homeric form of εἶ ‘you are’ (Attic εἶ), and θεράπων is an attendant, a retainer such as the Myrmidon Hermes has claimed to be. The command κατάλεξον ‘recount’ is followed by two alternatives, ἢ ἔτι … ἦέ … ἤδη, ‘whether … still … or whether … by now …’. ᾗσι κυσίν is ‘to his own dogs’ (ᾗσι is the epic dative plural of ἑός ‘his own’), μελεϊστί is ‘limb by limb’, ταμών the aorist participle of τέμνω ‘cut’, and προύθηκεν is προέθηκεν, ‘set out before’. Πηληϊάδεω is the epic genitive of the patronymic, and Ἀχιλῆος has one λ for the metre.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe diaktoros argeïphontēs·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the guide, Argeïphontes:
sentences.i: Then the guide, the slayer of Argus, said to him in turn:
sentences.n: Hermes answers. This whole-line speech introduction always has this English: διάκτορος ‘the guide’ is the god’s title as escort, and ἀργεϊφόντης ‘slayer of Argus’ is the usual explanation of a name whose meaning is disputed. αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks the exchange.

sentences.t:
ὦ γέρον οὔ πω τόν γε κύνες φάγον οὐδ’ οἰωνοί,
ἀλλ’ ἔτι κεῖνος κεῖται Ἀχιλλῆος παρὰ νηῒ
αὔτως ἐν κλισίῃσι·
sentences.tr:
ō geron ou pō ton ge kynes phagon oud’ oiōnoi,
all’ eti keinos keitai Achillēos para nēï
autōs en klisiēisi·
sentences.i: “Old man, neither dogs nor birds have eaten him yet; he still lies by Achilles’ ship, just as he was, among the huts;
sentences.n: Hermes speaks, and the answer is good news. τόν γε … κύνες φάγον is ‘dogs have eaten him’: φάγον is the aorist (Attic ἔφαγον) without its augment, and οὔ πω … οὐδ’ gives ‘not yet … nor’. κεῖνος is ‘that one’, Hector, and κεῖται ‘lies’ is the verb for a body laid out. αὔτως is ‘just so, as he was’. κλισίῃσι is the dative plural ‘huts’ of the camp (κλισίη), and Ἀχιλλῆος παρὰ νηῒ is ‘beside Achilles’ ship’, the ship drawn up on the shore with the hut near it.
sentences.mark: Hermes says the body is unharmed

sentences.t:
δυωδεκάτη δέ οἱ ἠὼς
κειμένῳ, οὐδέ τί οἱ χρὼς σήπεται, οὐδέ μιν εὐλαὶ
ἔσθουσ’, αἵ ῥά τε φῶτας ἀρηϊφάτους κατέδουσιν.
sentences.tr:
dyōdekatē de hoi ēōs
keimenōi, oude ti hoi chrōs sēpetai, oude min eulai
esthous’, hai rha te phōtas arēïphatous katedousin.
sentences.l:
and the twelfth dawn is upon him
lying there, and not at all does his skin rot, nor do the worms
eat him, which devour men slain in war.
sentences.i: and this is the twelfth dawn for him as he lies there, and his skin does not rot at all, nor do the worms eat him, the worms that devour men killed in war.
sentences.n: δυωδεκάτη … ἠὼς is ‘the twelfth dawn’, as the Greeks counted days by dawns; οἱ is ‘for him’, and κειμένῳ ‘as he lies’ agrees with it. χρώς is the skin, the body’s surface. εὐλαί are the worms or maggots that breed in a corpse. ἔσθουσ’ is ἔσθουσι, ‘eat’, and αἵ ῥά τε is ‘which, as is well known’. ἀρηϊφάτους is ‘killed in war’ (Ἄρης, the war-god, + a word for ‘slain’), and κατέδουσιν is ‘devour’.

sentences.t:
ἦ μέν μιν περὶ σῆμα ἑοῦ ἑτάροιο φίλοιο
ἕλκει ἀκηδέστως ἠὼς ὅτε δῖα φανήῃ,
οὐδέ μιν αἰσχύνει·
sentences.tr:
ē men min peri sēma heou hetaroio philoio
helkei akēdestōs ēōs hote dia phanēēi,
oude min aischynei·
sentences.i: Truly, whenever heavenly dawn appears, he drags him uncaringly around the tomb of his own dear companion, and does not disfigure him;
sentences.n: The companion is Patroclus, and Achilles has been dragging the body behind his chariot round Patroclus’ tomb each morning. ἦ μέν is ‘truly’. ἑοῦ ἑτάροιο φίλοιο is ‘his own dear companion’, with ἑοῦ the reflexive possessive; ἀκηδέστως ‘uncaringly’ is the adverb of the word for ‘uncaring’. ὅτε … φανήῃ is a general clause, ‘whenever … has appeared’, with φανήῃ a subjunctive. αἰσχύνει means ‘disfigures’, literally ‘makes ugly’.

sentences.t:
θηοῖό κεν αὐτὸς ἐπελθὼν
οἷον ἐερσήεις κεῖται, περὶ δ’ αἷμα νένιπται,
οὐδέ ποθι μιαρός·
sentences.tr:
thēoio ken autos epelthōn
hoion eersēeis keitai, peri d’ haima neniptai,
oude pothi miaros·
sentences.i: you would marvel yourself if you came near, to see how dewy he lies, with the blood washed from him, and not stained anywhere;
sentences.n: θηοῖο is the optative of θηέομαι ‘gaze in wonder’, and with κεν gives ‘you would marvel’; αὐτός means ‘yourself’, ‘if you saw it with your own eyes’. οἷον … κεῖται is ‘how … he lies’, and ἐερσήεις ‘dewy’ pictures a body still fresh. νένιπται is the perfect passive of νίζω ‘wash’. The last clause has no verb: οὐδέ ποθι μιαρός is ‘nor (is he) stained anywhere’, with μιαρός ‘stained’ by blood or dirt.

sentences.t:
σὺν δ’ ἕλκεα πάντα μέμυκεν
ὅσσ’ ἐτύπη·
sentences.tr:
syn d’ helkea panta memyken
hoss’ etypē·
sentences.l:
and all the wounds have closed together,
as many as were struck;
sentences.i: and all the wounds have closed up, as many as were dealt;
sentences.n: σὺν … μέμυκεν is one verb split in two, ‘have closed up’ (perfect of μύω ‘close’, used of lips and eyes). ἕλκεα is ‘wounds’ (Attic ἕλκη). ὅσσ’ ἐτύπη is ‘as many as were struck’: a neuter plural subject with a singular verb, as Greek allows, and ἐτύπη the aorist passive of τύπτω ‘strike’.

sentences.t: πολέες γὰρ ἐν αὐτῷ χαλκὸν ἔλασσαν.
sentences.tr: polees gar en autōi chalkon elassan.
sentences.l: for many drove bronze into him.
sentences.i: for many men drove bronze into him.
sentences.n: πολέες is the epic form of πολλοί ‘many’, the men who struck Hector, and αὐτῷ ‘in him’ is Hector. χαλκόν ‘bronze’ stands for the weapon. ἔλασσαν is ‘drove’, the epic aorist of ἐλαύνω, with doubled σ.

sentences.t:
ὥς τοι κήδονται μάκαρες θεοὶ υἷος ἑῆος
καὶ νέκυός περ ἐόντος, ἐπεί σφι φίλος περὶ κῆρι.
sentences.tr:
hōs toi kēdontai makares theoi huios heēos
kai nekyos per eontos, epei sphi philos peri kēri.
sentences.l:
So do the blessed gods care for your own son,
even though he is a corpse, since he was dear to them exceedingly in heart.”
sentences.i: That is how the blessed gods care for your own son, even though he is a corpse, since he was very dear to their hearts.”
sentences.n: ὥς τοι is ‘so, you see’: τοι is the ‘you see’ particle (the dative of σύ). κήδονται takes the genitive υἷος ‘son’ (Attic υἱοῦ), and ἑῆος is ‘your own’ (epic ἑός, ‘his own’, agreeing with υἷος, used here of the person addressed; ἑῆος could also be read as ἐῆος, ‘good’, but ‘own’ is taken here). καὶ νέκυός περ ἐόντος is ‘even though he is a corpse’, a genitive absolute. φίλος περὶ κῆρι is ‘dear exceedingly at heart’: περί is an adverb ‘exceedingly’, and κῆρι the dative of κῆρ ‘heart’; σφι is ‘to them’, the gods.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, γήθησεν δ’ ὃ γέρων, καὶ ἀμείβετο μύθῳ·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, gēthēsen d’ ho gerōn, kai ameibeto mythōi·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and the old man rejoiced, and answered with a word:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the old man rejoiced, and answered him:
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ closes Hermes’ speech; in ὃ γέρων the ὃ is the article used as a pronoun, ‘he, the old man’. γήθησεν is ‘rejoiced’, and ἀμείβετο μύθῳ is ‘answered with a word’; the line ends with a colon, because Priam’s speech follows.

sentences.t:
ὦ τέκος, ἦ ῥ’ ἀγαθὸν καὶ ἐναίσιμα δῶρα διδοῦναι
ἀθανάτοις, ἐπεὶ οὔ ποτ’ ἐμὸς πάϊς, εἴ ποτ’ ἔην γε,
λήθετ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροισι θεῶν οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσι·
sentences.tr:
ō tekos, ē rh’ agathon kai enaisima dōra didounai
athanatois, epei ou pot’ emos païs, ei pot’ eēn ge,
lēthet’ eni megaroisi theōn hoi Olympon echousi·
sentences.i: “My child, it is truly a good thing to give fitting gifts to the immortals, since my son — if ever he was — never forgot, in his halls, the gods who hold Olympus;
sentences.n: Priam, glad, speaks to the stranger. τέκος ‘child’ is a kindly way to address a young man. ἦ ῥ’ ἀγαθόν is ‘truly good’, with ἀγαθόν a neuter, ‘a good thing’, and the infinitive διδοῦναι ‘to give’ as its subject. ἐναίσιμα ‘fitting’ belongs to the αἶσα ‘due measure’ family. εἴ ποτ’ ἔην γε ‘if ever he was’ is Priam’s way of speaking of a son who may no longer be. λήθετ’ is ἐλήθετο (imperfect without the augment) of λανθάνομαι ‘forget’, which takes the genitive θεῶν. μεγάροισι is ‘in the halls’, the great rooms of a house.

sentences.t: τώ οἱ ἀπεμνήσαντο καὶ ἐν θανάτοιό περ αἴσῃ.
sentences.tr: tō hoi apemnēsanto kai en thanatoio per aisēi.
sentences.l: therefore for him they remembered in return, even in the portion of death.
sentences.i: and so they have remembered him in return, even in the lot of death.
sentences.n: τώ is ‘therefore, and so’. ἀπεμνήσαντο is the aorist middle of a compound of μιμνήσκω ‘remember’; the prefix ἀπο- may carry the sense ‘in return’, as if the gods were repaying Hector’s offerings. θανάτοιο is the epic genitive of θάνατος ‘death’, and αἶσα is the ‘lot’ or share that falls to each; περ ‘even’ stresses the extreme case.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ τόδε δέξαι ἐμεῦ πάρα καλὸν ἄλεισον,
sentences.tr: all’ age dē tode dexai emeu para kalon aleison,
sentences.l: But come now, accept this fair goblet from me,
sentences.i: But come now, accept this fair goblet from me,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή ‘but come now’ opens the request. δέξαι is the aorist imperative middle of δέχομαι ‘accept’. ἐμεῦ πάρα is ‘from me’: πάρα is παρά written with the accent on its first syllable when it follows the word it governs. ἄλεισον is a goblet, a drinking vessel, which is the gift Priam presses on the stranger.

sentences.t:
αὐτόν τε ῥῦσαι, πέμψον δέ με σύν γε θεοῖσιν,
ὄφρά κεν ἐς κλισίην Πηληϊάδεω ἀφίκωμαι.
sentences.tr:
auton te rhysai, pempson de me syn ge theoisin,
ophra ken es klisiēn Pēlēïadeō aphikōmai.
sentences.l:
and protect me myself, and send me with the gods,
so that I may come to the hut of Peleus’-son.”
sentences.i: and protect me myself, and send me on my way, with the gods’ help, so that I may reach the hut of Peleus’ son.”
sentences.n: αὐτόν is ‘me myself’, set against the gifts: he asks to be guarded in person. ῥῦσαι is the aorist imperative middle of ῥύομαι ‘protect’, and πέμψον ‘send’, here ‘escort’. σύν γε θεοῖσιν is ‘with the gods (to help)’. ὄφρα κεν … ἀφίκωμαι is a purpose clause, ‘so that I may reach’, with a subjunctive. The closing mark ends Priam’s speech; Hermes replies next.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe diaktoros argeïphontēs·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the guide, Argeïphontes:
sentences.i: Then the guide, the slayer of Argus, said to him in turn:
sentences.n: The same speech introduction as at 410, with the same English. Hermes replies to the offer of the goblet.

sentences.t:
πειρᾷ ἐμεῖο γεραιὲ νεωτέρου, οὐδέ με πείσεις,
ὅς με κέλῃ σέο δῶρα παρὲξ Ἀχιλῆα δέχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
peirāi emeio geraie neōterou, oude me peiseis,
hos me kelēi seo dōra parex Achilēa dechesthai.
sentences.l:
“You are testing me, old man, one younger than you, and you will not persuade me,
you who bid me accept your gifts, bypassing Achilles.
sentences.i: “You are testing me, old man, one younger than you, but you will not persuade me, when you tell me to take your gifts and bypass Achilles.
sentences.n: πειρᾷ is ‘you test’, the second person of πειράομαι, and ἐμεῖο νεωτέρου is ‘me, being younger’ (the genitive after πειράομαι, ἐμεῖο the epic form of ἐμοῦ). πείσεις is the future of πείθω ‘persuade’. ὅς με κέλῃ is ‘you who bid me’ (ὅς picks up the ‘you’ of the first clause; κέλῃ is κέλεαι). παρὲξ Ἀχιλῆα is ‘apart from, bypassing Achilles’: παρέξ takes the accusative, and the Greek says only ‘apart from Achilles’, and the sense is ‘without his knowledge’.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ δείδοικα καὶ αἰδέομαι περὶ κῆρι
συλεύειν, μή μοί τι κακὸν μετόπισθε γένηται.
sentences.tr:
ton men egō deidoika kai aideomai peri kēri
syleuein, mē moi ti kakon metopisthe genētai.
sentences.l:
Him I fear, and I am ashamed in my heart exceedingly
to rob, lest some evil befall me afterwards.
sentences.i: I fear him, and I shrink deeply, in my heart, from robbing him, lest some evil come to me afterwards.
sentences.n: τὸν μέν is Achilles, put first for emphasis. δείδοικα is the perfect of δείδω, with present sense ‘I fear’. αἰδέομαι is ‘feel respect, shame before’, and with the infinitive συλεύειν ‘rob’ it means ‘shrink from robbing’; περὶ κῆρι is ‘exceedingly in heart’, as at 423. μή … γένηται is a clause of fear, ‘lest … befall’, and μετόπισθε is ‘afterwards’. συλεύειν ‘rob, strip’ is Hermes’ word for taking the gifts without Achilles’ knowledge, a risk he says he fears.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ ἂν ἐγὼ πομπὸς καί κε κλυτὸν Ἄργος ἱκοίμην,
ἐνδυκέως ἐν νηῒ θοῇ ἢ πεζὸς ὁμαρτέων·
sentences.tr:
soi d’ an egō pompos kai ke klyton Argos hikoimēn,
endykeōs en nēï thoēi ē pezos homarteōn·
sentences.l:
But for you as escort I would go even to famous Argos,
kindly, on a swift ship or on foot accompanying you;
sentences.i: But as your escort I would go even to famous Argos, kindly, whether in a swift ship or going along with you on foot;
sentences.n: σοὶ δ’ ἂν ἐγώ … ἱκοίμην is ‘but I for you … would go’, an optative with ἄν. πομπός is an ‘escort’, one who sees a traveller on his way (accusative πομπόν at 439). Ἄργος here is a distant Greek land, so the offer is a generous exaggeration. ἐνδυκέως is ‘kindly’, and ἢ gives the alternative ‘in a swift ship or on foot’. πεζός is ‘on foot’, and ὁμαρτέων is the participle of ὁμαρτέω ‘go along with’.

sentences.t: οὐκ ἄν τίς τοι πομπὸν ὀνοσσάμενος μαχέσαιτο.
sentences.tr: ouk an tis toi pompon onossamenos machesaito.
sentences.l: no one would fight you, making light of your escort.”
sentences.i: No one would make light of your escort and attack you.”
sentences.n: οὐκ ἄν τις is ‘no one would’. ὀνοσσάμενος is the aorist participle of ὄνομαι ‘find fault with, make light of’, here with the object πομπόν ‘escort’; μαχέσαιτο is the optative of μάχομαι ‘fight’. The closing mark ends Hermes’ speech.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ ἀναΐξας ἐριούνιος ἅρμα καὶ ἵππους
καρπαλίμως μάστιγα καὶ ἡνία λάζετο χερσίν,
sentences.tr:
ē kai anaïxas eriounios harma kai hippous
karpalimōs mastiga kai hēnia lazeto chersin,
sentences.l:
He spoke, and the helper, having sprung up onto the chariot and horses,
swiftly the whip and the reins took in his hands,
sentences.i: So he said, and the helper sprang up to the chariot and horses and quickly took the whip and the reins in his hands,
sentences.n: ἦ καὶ is a formula for ‘he spoke and’. ἀναΐξας is ‘having sprung up’; ἅρμα καὶ ἵππους is the chariot with its horses, the whole team. ἐριούνιος is a name for Hermes whose meaning is unknown; ‘the helper’ is one ancient guess. λάζετο is ‘took’ (imperfect of λάζομαι), and μάστιγα καὶ ἡνία is ‘the whip and the reins’, here in his hands (χερσίν).

sentences.t: ἐν δ’ ἔπνευσ’ ἵπποισι καὶ ἡμιόνοις μένος ἠΰ.
sentences.tr: en d’ epneus’ hippoisi kai hēmionois menos ēÿ.
sentences.l: and breathed into horses and mules good might.
sentences.i: and breathed good might into the horses and mules.
sentences.n: ἐν … ἔπνευσ’ is one verb split in two: ‘breathed into’ (ἐμπνέω). μένος is ‘might’ and ἠΰ is the neuter of ἐΰς ‘good’, so ‘good might’; a god adds strength to the animals.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ πύργους τε νεῶν καὶ τάφρον ἵκοντο,
οἳ δὲ νέον περὶ δόρπα φυλακτῆρες πονέοντο,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē pyrgous te neōn kai taphron hikonto,
hoi de neon peri dorpa phylaktēres poneonto,
sentences.l:
But when they came to the towers of the ships and the ditch,
and the sentries were just then busy about their supper,
sentences.i: But when they reached the towers by the ships and the ditch, the sentries were just then busy about their supper,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή is ‘but when’. πύργους … νεῶν καὶ τάφρον are the defences of the Achaean camp, the towers built along the wall, and the ditch outside. ἵκοντο is ‘they came’ (ἱκνέομαι, without augment). οἳ δέ is ‘and they’, the guards; φυλακτῆρες ‘sentries’, and νέον ‘just now’. πονέοντο is the imperfect of πονέομαι ‘labour, be busy’, uncontracted. The clause leads to the main verb at 445.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἐφ’ ὕπνον ἔχευε διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης
πᾶσιν, ἄφαρ δ’ ὤϊξε πύλας καὶ ἀπῶσεν ὀχῆας,
sentences.tr:
toisi d’ eph’ hypnon echeue diaktoros argeïphontēs
pasin, aphar d’ ōïxe pylas kai apōsen ochēas,
sentences.l:
upon them all sleep poured the guide, Argeïphontes,
and at once he opened the gates and thrust back the bars,
sentences.i: the guide, the slayer of Argus, poured sleep over all of them, and at once he opened the gates and thrust back the bars,
sentences.n: τοῖσι is ‘upon them’, the sentries, and πᾶσιν ‘all’ comes after the verb for emphasis. ἐφ’ ὕπνον ἔχευε is ‘poured sleep upon’ (ἐπέχευε, a split verb). ὤϊξε is the aorist of ἀνοίγνυμι ‘open’ in its epic form, and ἀπῶσεν the aorist of ἀπωθέω ‘push away’. ὀχῆας is ‘bars’, the heavy beams that closed the gates; the gates are those of the camp wall.

sentences.t: ἐς δ’ ἄγαγε Πρίαμόν τε καὶ ἀγλαὰ δῶρ’ ἐπ’ ἀπήνης.
sentences.tr: es d’ agage Priamon te kai aglaa dōr’ ep’ apēnēs.
sentences.l: and led in Priam and the splendid gifts on the wagon.
sentences.i: and brought in Priam and the splendid gifts on the wagon.
sentences.n: ἐς δ’ ἄγαγε is ‘and led in’ (ἐσήγαγε, a split verb). ἀγλαὰ δῶρ’ is ‘splendid gifts’, the ransom, and ἐπ’ ἀπήνης is ‘on the wagon’ (ἐπί with the genitive of ἀπήνη), the mule-wagon on which they have been riding.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ κλισίην Πηληϊάδεω ἀφίκοντο
ὑψηλήν, τὴν Μυρμιδόνες ποίησαν ἄνακτι
δοῦρ’ ἐλάτης κέρσαντες·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē klisiēn Pēlēïadeō aphikonto
hypsēlēn, tēn Myrmidones poiēsan anakti
dour’ elatēs kersantes·
sentences.i: But when they came to the hut of Peleus’ son, the high one, which the Myrmidons had made for their lord by cutting beams of fir;
sentences.n: ἀφίκοντο is ‘they arrived’. ὑψηλήν ‘high’ agrees with κλισίην ‘hut’, and the relative clause τὴν Μυρμιδόνες ποίησαν says who built it: the Myrmidons, the men Achilles leads. ἄνακτι is ‘for their lord’, and δοῦρ’ ἐλάτης is ‘beams (δοῦρα, plural of δόρυ) of fir’, the tree being ἐλάτη. κέρσαντες is the aorist participle of κείρω ‘cut’.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ καθύπερθεν ἔρεψαν
λαχνήεντ’ ὄροφον λειμωνόθεν ἀμήσαντες·
sentences.tr:
atar kathyperthen erepsan
lachnēent’ orophon leimōnothen amēsantes·
sentences.l:
and on top they roofed it with a shaggy thatch,
having mown it from the meadow;
sentences.i: and on top they roofed it with a shaggy thatch that they had mown from the meadow;
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘and, moreover’, and καθύπερθεν ‘on top’. ἔρεψαν is the aorist of ἐρέφω ‘roof’. ὄροφος is the roofing material, a thatch of reeds or grass, in the accusative; λαχνήεντ’ ‘shaggy’ describes it. λειμωνόθεν is ‘from the meadow’ (-θεν marks where it comes from), and ἀμήσαντες the aorist participle of ἀμάω ‘mow’.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ μεγάλην αὐλὴν ποίησαν ἄνακτι
σταυροῖσιν πυκινοῖσι·
sentences.tr:
amphi de hoi megalēn aulēn poiēsan anakti
stauroisin pykinoisi·
sentences.l:
and around it for him a great courtyard they made for their lord
with close-set stakes;
sentences.i: and around it they made for their lord a great courtyard of close-set stakes;
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ is ‘and around it’, with οἱ ‘for him’ pointing at Achilles and ἄνακτι repeating it. αὐλή is the courtyard enclosed by a fence of upright stakes (σταυροῖσιν, dative plural of σταυρός). πυκινοῖσι ‘close-set’ is the same word as ‘thick’, here of stakes planted close together.

sentences.t:
θύρην δ’ ἔχε μοῦνος ἐπιβλὴς
εἰλάτινος, τὸν τρεῖς μὲν ἐπιρρήσσεσκον Ἀχαιοί,
sentences.tr:
thyrēn d’ eche mounos epiblēs
eilatinos, ton treis men epirrēsseskon Achaioi,
sentences.l:
and a single cross-bar held the door,
of fir, which three Achaeans used to drive home,
sentences.i: and a single cross-bar of fir held the door shut, which three Achaeans would drive home,
sentences.n: θύρην is the door of the courtyard, the gate in the stakes, and it is the object: ἐπιβλής, the cross-bar laid across the gate, is the subject of ἔχε ‘held’, and μοῦνος is ‘single’. εἰλάτινος is ‘of fir’, the adjective of ἐλάτη. ἐπιρρήσσεσκον is the iterative imperfect ‘used to slam to, drive home’: the -σκ- ending marks what happened again and again. τρεῖς … Ἀχαιοί is ‘three Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
τρεῖς δ’ ἀναοίγεσκον μεγάλην κληῗδα θυράων
τῶν ἄλλων·
sentences.tr:
treis d’ anaoigeskon megalēn klēïda thyraōn
tōn allōn·
sentences.l:
and three would open the great bolt of the door
of the rest;
sentences.i: while three of the others would open the great bolt of the door;
sentences.n: ἀναοίγεσκον is another iterative, ‘used to open’. κληῗδα (κληΐς) is the bolt, the fastening that the cross-bar works. τῶν ἄλλων ‘of the others’ most likely goes with τρεῖς, ‘three of the other Achaeans’, as the English has it, but it could also go with θυράων and mean the door ‘of the rest’, the ordinary Achaeans’ doors; the Greek leaves both open. The point is that it took three men to open what Achilles shut alone.

sentences.t: Ἀχιλεὺς δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπιρρήσσεσκε καὶ οἶος·
sentences.tr: Achileus d’ ar’ epirrēsseske kai oios·
sentences.l: but Achilles used to drive it home even alone;
sentences.i: but Achilles would drive it home even by himself;
sentences.n: Ἀχιλεὺς δ’ ἄρ’ marks the contrast, ‘but Achilles’, with ἄρα marking the surprise. ἐπιρρήσσεσκε is the same iterative as above. καὶ οἶος is ‘even alone’: the contrast shows how strong he is.

sentences.t:
δή ῥα τόθ’ Ἑρμείας ἐριούνιος ᾦξε γέροντι,
ἐς δ’ ἄγαγε κλυτὰ δῶρα ποδώκεϊ Πηλεΐωνι,
sentences.tr:
dē rha toth’ Hermeias eriounios ōixe geronti,
es d’ agage klyta dōra podōkeï Pēleïōni,
sentences.l:
Then indeed Hermes the helper opened it for the old man,
and led in the famous gifts for swift-footed Peleus’ son,
sentences.i: Then Hermes the helper opened it for the old man and brought in the famous gifts for swift-footed Peleus’ son,
sentences.n: δή ῥα τόθ’ is ‘then indeed’. ᾦξε is ‘opened’, from the same verb as ὤϊξε at 446 in another spelling, and γέροντι ‘for the old man’. ἐριούνιος ‘the helper’ is Hermes’ name, of unknown meaning; ‘helper’ is one ancient guess. ἐς δ’ ἄγαγε is ‘and led in’; κλυτά ‘famous’ describes the gifts, and ποδώκεϊ ‘swift-footed’ is Achilles’ epithet, the dative of ποδώκης. Πηλεΐωνι is the patronymic ‘son of Peleus’, in the dative.

sentences.t: ἐξ ἵππων δ’ ἀπέβαινεν ἐπὶ χθόνα φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: ex hippōn d’ apebainen epi chthona phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: and from the horses he stepped down to the earth and spoke:
sentences.i: He stepped down from the horses to the ground and spoke:
sentences.n: ἀπέβαινεν is ‘stepped down’, the imperfect of ἀποβαίνω; ἐξ ἵππων is ‘from the horses’, meaning from the chariot he is standing on. φώνησε is ‘spoke’ (the verb of speaking aloud), and the line ends with a colon.

sentences.t:
ὦ γέρον ἤτοι ἐγὼ θεὸς ἄμβροτος εἰλήλουθα
Ἑρμείας·
sentences.tr:
ō geron ētoi egō theos ambrotos eilēloutha
Hermeias·
sentences.l:
“Old man, I indeed, a deathless god, have come —
Hermes;
sentences.i: “Old man, I am a deathless god who has come — Hermes;
sentences.n: Hermes declares himself. ἤτοι ἐγώ is ‘I indeed’, with ἤτοι printed as one word. ἄμβροτος is ‘deathless’ (ἀ- ‘not’ + βροτός ‘mortal’). εἰλήλουθα is the perfect of ἔρχομαι, ‘I have come’ (Attic ἐλήλυθα). The name Ἑρμείας comes in the second line, after the verb, so the reveal is delayed.

sentences.t: σοὶ γάρ με πατὴρ ἅμα πομπὸν ὄπασσεν.
sentences.tr: soi gar me patēr hama pompon opassen.
sentences.l: for my father gave me along to you as escort.
sentences.i: for my father sent me along with you as your escort.
sentences.n: Hermes’ father is Zeus, who sent him in the last part. σοί … με … ἅμα πομπόν is ‘me along with you as escort’; ὄπασσεν is the aorist of ὀπάζω ‘give as an attendant’, with doubled σ for the metre.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι μὲν ἐγὼ πάλιν εἴσομαι, οὐδ’ Ἀχιλῆος
ὀφθαλμοὺς εἴσειμι·
sentences.tr:
all’ ētoi men egō palin eisomai, oud’ Achilēos
ophthalmous eiseimi·
sentences.l:
But I indeed shall go back again, and into Achilles’
eyes I shall not go;
sentences.i: But I shall go back again, and I shall not go before Achilles’ eyes;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι μὲν ἐγώ is ‘but I, for my part’. εἴσομαι here is a future of the verb of going, ‘I shall go’, and πάλιν ‘back’. οὐδ’ … ὀφθαλμοὺς εἴσειμι is ‘nor shall I go into the eyes of’, a way of saying ‘come before him’: εἴσειμι is ‘I shall go in’. Ἀχιλῆος has a single λ.

sentences.t:
νεμεσσητὸν δέ κεν εἴη
ἀθάνατον θεὸν ὧδε βροτοὺς ἀγαπαζέμεν ἄντην·
sentences.tr:
nemessēton de ken eiē
athanaton theon hōde brotous agapazemen antēn·
sentences.l:
and it would be a thing to resent
that an immortal god should thus welcome mortals face to face;
sentences.i: and it would be a thing to resent for an immortal god to welcome mortals like this, face to face;
sentences.n: νεμεσσητόν is ‘a thing to resent’, κεν εἴη is ‘it would be’. ἀθάνατον θεὸν is the subject of the infinitive, ‘an immortal god’, and ὧδε ‘thus, so’. ἀγαπαζέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἀγαπάζω ‘welcome’, and ἄντην is ‘face to face’.

sentences.t: τύνη δ’ εἰσελθὼν λαβὲ γούνατα Πηλεΐωνος,
sentences.tr: tynē d’ eiselthōn labe gounata Pēleïōnos,
sentences.l: But you, going in, take hold of the knees of Peleus’-son,
sentences.i: But you go in and take hold of the knees of Peleus’ son,
sentences.n: τύνη is an emphatic ‘you yourself’, a form of σύ. λαβέ is the aorist imperative of λαμβάνω, and λαβὲ γούνατα is ‘take hold of the knees’, the suppliant’s gesture; εἰσελθών is ‘having gone in’. Πηλεΐωνος is ‘of Peleus’ son’, the genitive.

sentences.t:
καί μιν ὑπὲρ πατρὸς καὶ μητέρος ἠϋκόμοιο
λίσσεο καὶ τέκεος, ἵνα οἱ σὺν θυμὸν ὀρίνῃς.
sentences.tr:
kai min hyper patros kai mēteros ēÿkomoio
lisseo kai tekeos, hina hoi syn thymon orinēis.
sentences.l:
and beseech him by his father and his fine-haired mother
and his child, so that you may stir his heart.”
sentences.i: and beg him in the name of his father, and of his fine-haired mother, and of his child, so that you may stir his heart.”
sentences.n: λίσσεο is the imperative of λίσσομαι ‘beseech’, and ὑπὲρ πατρός … καὶ τέκεος is ‘in the name of his father … and his child’; τέκεος is the epic genitive of τέκος. The mother is Thetis, and ἠϋκόμοιο is ‘fine-haired’ (genitive). Hermes is naming those Achilles loves best, the father and the child he has left behind. ἵνα οἱ σὺν θυμὸν ὀρίνῃς is a purpose clause, with the verb split (σὺν … ὀρίνῃς, ‘stir together’); θυμός is ‘heart’ and ὀρίνω ‘stir’. The closing mark ends Hermes’ speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη πρὸς μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον
Ἑρμείας·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsas apebē pros makron Olympon
Hermeias·
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, went away to tall Olympus
Hermes;
sentences.i: With these words Hermes went away to tall Olympus;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη is a formula, ‘so then, having spoken, he went away’. μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον is ‘tall Olympus’, the mountain of the gods. The subject Ἑρμείας comes last in the sentence, and the semicolon after it starts a new thought with Priam.

sentences.t:
Πρίαμος δ’ ἐξ ἵππων ἆλτο χαμᾶζε,
Ἰδαῖον δὲ κατ’ αὖθι λίπεν·
sentences.tr:
Priamos d’ ex hippōn alto chamaze,
Idaion de kat’ authi lipen·
sentences.l:
and Priam leapt from the horses to the ground,
but Idaeus he left there on the spot;
sentences.i: and Priam leapt from the chariot to the ground, but Idaeus he left there on the spot;
sentences.n: Πρίαμος δ’ is ‘and Priam’. ἐξ ἵππων is ‘from the horses’, meaning from the chariot. ἆλτο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’, and χαμᾶζε ‘to the ground’ takes the suffix -ζε for direction. Idaeus is Priam’s herald; κατ’ αὖθι is ‘right there’, and λίπεν the aorist of λείπω ‘leave’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ μίμνεν ἐρύκων
ἵππους ἡμιόνους τε·
sentences.tr:
ho de mimnen erykōn
hippous hēmionous te·
sentences.l:
and he stayed, holding back
the horses and mules;
sentences.i: and he stayed behind, holding back the horses and mules;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is ‘and he’, Idaeus. μίμνεν is the imperfect of μίμνω ‘stay’, and ἐρύκων the participle ‘holding back, keeping in check’. ἵππους ἡμιόνους τε are the chariot’s horses and the wagon’s mules.

sentences.t:
γέρων δ’ ἰθὺς κίεν οἴκου,
τῇ ῥ’ Ἀχιλεὺς ἵζεσκε Διῒ φίλος·
sentences.tr:
gerōn d’ ithys kien oikou,
tēi rh’ Achileus hizeske Diï philos·
sentences.l:
and the old man went straight toward the house,
where Achilles, dear to Zeus, used to sit;
sentences.i: and the old man went straight toward the house where Achilles, dear to Zeus, used to sit;
sentences.n: γέρων is Priam. ἰθὺς … οἴκου is ‘straight toward the house’, with the genitive of the place aimed at. κίεν is ‘went’, and τῇ ῥ’ … ἵζεσκε ‘where he used to sit’, an iterative imperfect of ἵζω. Διῒ φίλος ‘dear to Zeus’ is Achilles’ stock epithet here. The ‘house’ is the hut just described.

sentences.t:
ἐν δέ μιν αὐτὸν
εὗρ’, ἕταροι δ’ ἀπάνευθε καθήατο·
sentences.tr:
en de min auton
heur’, hetaroi d’ apaneuthe kathēato·
sentences.l:
and within, him himself
he found, and his companions sat apart;
sentences.i: and inside he found Achilles himself, while his companions sat apart;
sentences.n: ἐν is ‘within’. μιν αὐτόν is ‘him himself’, Achilles in person; εὗρ’ is the aorist of εὑρίσκω ‘find’. ἕταροι ‘companions’ is the Homeric ἑταῖροι, and καθήατο is the old form of ἐκάθηντο ‘were sitting’. ἀπάνευθε is ‘apart’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ δύ’ οἴω
ἥρως Αὐτομέδων τε καὶ Ἄλκιμος ὄζος Ἄρηος
ποίπνυον παρεόντε·
sentences.tr:
tō de dy’ oiō
hērōs Automedōn te kai Alkimos ozos Arēos
poipnyon pareonte·
sentences.i: and only the two of them, the hero Automedon and Alcimus, scion of Ares, bustled about, standing by;
sentences.n: τὼ δὲ δύ’ οἴω is ‘but the two alone’, a dual phrase (τώ is the dual article). Automedon and Alcimus are Achilles’ charioteer and a close companion. ὄζος Ἄρηος ‘scion of Ares’ is a stock title; ὄζος is literally ‘branch’. ποίπνυον is the imperfect (plural) of ποιπνύω ‘bustle about, serve’, and παρεόντε is a dual participle ‘being near’, because it speaks of two men.

sentences.t:
νέον δ’ ἀπέληγεν ἐδωδῆς
ἔσθων καὶ πίνων·
sentences.tr:
neon d’ apelēgen edōdēs
esthōn kai pinōn·
sentences.l:
and he had only just ceased from food,
eating and drinking;
sentences.i: and he had only just stopped eating and drinking;
sentences.n: νέον is ‘just now’, and ἀπέληγεν is ‘had stopped’ (imperfect of ἀπολήγω) and takes the genitive ἐδωδῆς ‘food’. The subject is Achilles. ἔσθων καὶ πίνων is ‘eating and drinking’, the participle added to say how he had been occupied.

sentences.t: ἔτι καὶ παρέκειτο τράπεζα.
sentences.tr: eti kai parekeito trapeza.
sentences.l: still too the table stood beside him.
sentences.i: the table was still standing by him.
sentences.n: ἔτι καὶ is ‘still also’, and παρέκειτο is ‘lay beside’, the imperfect of παράκειμαι. τράπεζα is the table still set, so Priam comes on a man only just done with his meal.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ ἔλαθ’ εἰσελθὼν Πρίαμος μέγας, ἄγχι δ’ ἄρα στὰς
χερσὶν Ἀχιλλῆος λάβε γούνατα καὶ κύσε χεῖρας
δεινὰς ἀνδροφόνους, αἵ οἱ πολέας κτάνον υἷας.
sentences.tr:
tous d’ elath’ eiselthōn Priamos megas, anchi d’ ara stas
chersin Achillēos labe gounata kai kyse cheiras
deinas androphonous, hai hoi poleas ktanon huias.
sentences.l:
Unnoticed by them Priam the great came in, and standing close,
with his hands took hold of Achilles’ knees and kissed his hands,
terrible, man-slaying, which killed many of his sons.
sentences.i: Great Priam came in without being seen by them, and standing close, took hold of Achilles’ knees in his hands and kissed his hands, the terrible, man-slaying hands that had killed many of his sons.
sentences.n: τοὺς δ’ ἔλαθ’ εἰσελθών is ‘and he escaped their notice, having come in’: ἔλαθε takes the accusative, and εἰσελθών is the participle. Πρίαμος μέγας is ‘great Priam’. ἄγχι … στάς is ‘having stood close by’. χερσίν … λάβε γούνατα is ‘with his hands took hold of the knees’, the suppliant’s grip as at 465. κύσε is the aorist of κυνέω ‘kiss’; he kisses the hands that killed his sons. δεινάς ‘terrible’ and ἀνδροφόνους ‘man-slaying’ both agree with χεῖρας ‘hands’ in the line before. αἵ οἱ is ‘which … his’; οἱ is a dative of possession. πολέας is the epic form of πολλούς. κτάνον is the aorist of κτείνω ‘kill’, without augment. (This unit runs on across the line end because the pinned source has no stop after χεῖρας.)

sentences.t: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἄνδρ’ ἄτη πυκινὴ λάβῃ,
sentences.tr: hōs d’ hot’ an andr’ atē pykinē labēi,
sentences.l: And as when thick bewilderment seizes a man,
sentences.i: As when thick bewilderment seizes a man,
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν opens a simile: ‘as when …’. ἄτη is ‘bewilderment’, the mind’s blindness that lets a man do a terrible thing; πυκινή ‘thick, dense’ stresses how heavily it falls. λάβῃ is a subjunctive after ὅτ’ ἂν, because the picture is a general one.

sentences.t:
ὅς τ’ ἐνὶ πάτρῃ
φῶτα κατακτείνας ἄλλων ἐξίκετο δῆμον
ἀνδρὸς ἐς ἀφνειοῦ,
sentences.tr:
hos t’ eni patrēi
phōta katakteinas allōn exiketo dēmon
andros es aphneiou,
sentences.l:
who in his native land
having killed a man comes to the land of others,
to the house of a rich man,
sentences.i: who has killed a man in his native land and comes to the country of others, to the house of a rich man,
sentences.n: ὅς τ’ is ‘who, as happens’. ἐνὶ πάτρῃ is ‘in his native land’ (Attic ἐν πατρίδι). φῶτα κατακτείνας is ‘having killed a man’, a murder which makes him an exile. ἄλλων … δῆμον ‘the country of others’ takes ἐξίκετο ‘he comes’ (aorist of a general sense). ἀνδρὸς ἐς ἀφνειοῦ is ‘to a rich man’s’, with ‘house’ left unsaid. A man who had killed and fled his own country was received into a stranger’s house.

sentences.t: θάμβος δ’ ἔχει εἰσορόωντας,
sentences.tr: thambos d’ echei eisoroōntas,
sentences.l: and wonder holds those looking at him,
sentences.i: and wonder holds those who look at him,
sentences.n: θάμβος is ‘wonder’, the stunned silence of the household. ἔχει is ‘holds’, and εἰσορόωντας is the accusative participle ‘looking on’. The simile ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς Ἀχιλεὺς θάμβησεν ἰδὼν Πρίαμον θεοειδέα·
sentences.tr: hōs Achileus thambēsen idōn Priamon theoeidea·
sentences.l: so Achilles was struck with wonder, seeing Priam, godlike in form;
sentences.i: so Achilles was struck with wonder at the sight of Priam, godlike in form;
sentences.n: ὣς answers the simile’s ὡς, ‘so’. θάμβησεν is ‘was struck with wonder’, from the same family as θάμβος. θεοειδέα is the accusative of θεοειδής ‘godlike in form’, Priam’s stock epithet. The simile compares Priam to the exile arriving at a strange house, and Achilles to the household struck dumb at the sight of him, though here it is the host who has killed.

sentences.t: θάμβησαν δὲ καὶ ἄλλοι, ἐς ἀλλήλους δὲ ἴδοντο.
sentences.tr: thambēsan de kai alloi, es allēlous de idonto.
sentences.l: and the others too were struck with wonder, and looked at one another.
sentences.i: and the others too were struck with wonder, and looked at one another.
sentences.n: θάμβησαν is the plural of θάμβησεν above. ἄλλοι ‘the others’ are Achilles’ companions, and ἐς ἀλλήλους δὲ ἴδοντο is ‘and they looked at one another’; ἴδοντο is the aorist middle of ὁράω.

sentences.t: τὸν καὶ λισσόμενος Πρίαμος πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.tr: ton kai lissomenos Priamos pros mython eeipe·
sentences.l: Him also, begging, Priam addressed with a word:
sentences.i: And Priam, begging, spoke to him:
sentences.n: τὸν is Achilles. λισσόμενος is ‘begging’, the participle of λίσσομαι, and πρὸς … ἔειπε is ‘addressed, spoke to’ with the verb split. καὶ is a small particle, ‘also’, in the formula, and the line ends with a colon before Priam’s supplication.

sentences.t:
μνῆσαι πατρὸς σοῖο θεοῖς ἐπιείκελ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ,
τηλίκου ὥς περ ἐγών, ὀλοῷ ἐπὶ γήραος οὐδῷ·
sentences.tr:
mnēsai patros soio theois epieikel’ Achilleu,
tēlikou hōs per egōn, oloōi epi gēraos oudōi·
sentences.l:
“Remember your father, resembling the gods, Achilles,
of the same age as I, on the baneful threshold of old age;
sentences.i: “Remember your father, Achilles, you who are like the gods, one of my own age, on the baneful threshold of old age;
sentences.n: Priam’s speech to Achilles begins with the thing he knows will move him most, his own father. μνῆσαι is the aorist imperative middle of μιμνήσκω ‘remember’, taking the genitive πατρός. θεοῖς ἐπιείκελ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ is ‘Achilles, resembling the gods’, a vocative formula. τηλίκου ὥς περ ἐγών is ‘of just such an age as I’, and ὀλοῷ ‘baneful’ goes with οὐδῷ ‘threshold’: old age is the threshold of death. γήραος is the epic genitive of γῆρας ‘old age’.

sentences.t:
καὶ μέν που κεῖνον περιναιέται ἀμφὶς ἐόντες
τείρουσ’,
sentences.tr:
kai men pou keinon perinaietai amphis eontes
teirous’,
sentences.l:
And perhaps even him those who dwell around
are wearing down,
sentences.i: And perhaps the people who live around him are wearing him down,
sentences.n: καὶ μέν που is ‘and I suppose’. κεῖνον is Achilles’ father, Peleus, in the accusative; περιναιέται ἀμφὶς ἐόντες is ‘those dwelling around, being on every side’, neighbours. τείρουσ’ is τείρουσι, ‘wear down, distress’. Peleus is far away in Phthia.

sentences.t: οὐδέ τίς ἐστιν ἀρὴν καὶ λοιγὸν ἀμῦναι.
sentences.tr: oude tis estin arēn kai loigon amynai.
sentences.l: and there is no one to ward off harm and ruin.
sentences.i: and there is no one to ward off harm and ruin from him.
sentences.n: οὐδέ τίς ἐστιν … ἀμῦναι is ‘and there is no one to …’, an infinitive of purpose after ἐστιν. ἀμῦναι is the aorist infinitive of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’. ἀρήν is the accusative of ἀρή ‘harm’, and λοιγόν is ‘ruin’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι κεῖνός γε σέθεν ζώοντος ἀκούων
χαίρει τ’ ἐν θυμῷ,
sentences.tr:
all’ ētoi keinos ge sethen zōontos akouōn
chairei t’ en thymōi,
sentences.l:
But that man, at least, hearing that you are alive,
rejoices in his heart,
sentences.i: But he, at least, rejoices in his heart when he hears you are alive,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι κεῖνός γε is ‘but he, indeed’, a contrast with the lack of defenders. σέθεν ζώοντος ἀκούων is ‘hearing of you living’: ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person heard of, and ζώοντος agrees with σέθεν, the epic genitive of σύ. χαίρει τ’ ἐν θυμῷ is ‘rejoices in his heart’.

sentences.t:
ἐπί τ’ ἔλπεται ἤματα πάντα
ὄψεσθαι φίλον υἱὸν ἀπὸ Τροίηθεν ἰόντα·
sentences.tr:
epi t’ elpetai ēmata panta
opsesthai philon huion apo Troiēthen ionta·
sentences.l:
and hopes all his days
to see his dear son coming from Troy;
sentences.i: and hopes, for all his days, to see his dear son coming home from Troy;
sentences.n: ἐπί τ’ ἔλπεται is ‘and hopes’: ἐπί … ἔλπεται is one verb (ἐπέλπομαι) with τε between. ἤματα πάντα is ‘all his days’. ὄψεσθαι is the future infinitive ‘to see’, Τροίηθεν ‘from Troy’ takes the suffix -θεν ‘from’, and ἰόντα is ‘going, coming’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ πανάποτμος, ἐπεὶ τέκον υἷας ἀρίστους
Τροίῃ ἐν εὐρείῃ, τῶν δ’ οὔ τινά φημι λελεῖφθαι.
sentences.tr:
autar egō panapotmos, epei tekon huias aristous
Troiēi en eureiēi, tōn d’ ou tina phēmi leleiphthai.
sentences.l:
But I utterly ill-fated, since I begot the best sons
in wide Troy, and of them not one, I say, is left.
sentences.i: But I am utterly ill-fated: I fathered the best of sons in wide Troy, and I say that none of them is left.
sentences.n: Priam contrasts himself with Peleus: Peleus hopes, but Priam has nothing left. πανάποτμος is ‘utterly ill-fated’, a compound of πᾶν ‘all’ + ἄποτμος ‘ill-fated’. ἐπεὶ τέκον is ‘since I begot’, a reason for his misery, and ἀρίστους ‘the best’. These two lines repeat Priam’s own words at 24.255–256, where they follow ὤ μοι. λελεῖφθαι is the perfect passive infinitive ‘to be left’ (λείπω).

sentences.t: πεντήκοντά μοι ἦσαν ὅτ’ ἤλυθον υἷες Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr: pentēkonta moi ēsan hot’ ēlython huies Achaiōn·
sentences.l: Fifty I had when the sons of the Achaeans came;
sentences.i: I had fifty sons when the sons of the Achaeans came;
sentences.n: πεντήκοντά μοι ἦσαν is ‘fifty were to me’, the Greek way of saying ‘I had’; ‘sons’ is understood from the sense of υἷας in the line before. ἤλυθον is ‘came’, an alternative to ἦλθον, and υἷες Ἀχαιῶν is ‘the sons of the Achaeans’, a phrase for the whole army.

sentences.t:
ἐννεακαίδεκα μέν μοι ἰῆς ἐκ νηδύος ἦσαν,
τοὺς δ’ ἄλλους μοι ἔτικτον ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γυναῖκες.
sentences.tr:
enneakaideka men moi iēs ek nēdyos ēsan,
tous d’ allous moi etikton eni megaroisi gynaikes.
sentences.l:
nineteen were to me from one womb,
and the others women bore to me in my halls.
sentences.i: nineteen of them came from one womb, and the rest the women of my halls bore me.
sentences.n: ἐννεακαίδεκα is ‘nineteen’; ἰῆς is the Homeric feminine genitive of εἷς, ‘one’ (Attic μιᾶς), so ‘from one womb’ (Hecuba’s, though the Greek does not name her). νηδύς is ‘womb’. τοὺς δ’ ἄλλους is ‘the others’, and γυναῖκες ἐνὶ μεγάροισι ‘women in the halls’, the king’s other wives or concubines. ἔτικτον is an imperfect used for the past ‘bore’.

sentences.t: τῶν μὲν πολλῶν θοῦρος Ἄρης ὑπὸ γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν·
sentences.tr: tōn men pollōn thouros Arēs hypo gounat’ elysen·
sentences.l: Of the many of them impetuous Ares loosed the knees;
sentences.i: Impetuous Ares loosed the knees of the many of them;
sentences.n: τῶν μὲν πολλῶν is ‘of those, the many’, most of the sons. θοῦρος Ἄρης is ‘impetuous Ares’, the war-god standing for war. ὑπὸ γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν, literally ‘loosed (the) knees beneath’, is the stock phrase for killing a man: his knees give way. ὑπό is an adverb ‘beneath’, and the phrase is rendered ‘loosed the knees’, as at its other occurrences.

sentences.t:
ὃς δέ μοι οἶος ἔην, εἴρυτο δὲ ἄστυ καὶ αὐτούς,
τὸν σὺ πρῴην κτεῖνας ἀμυνόμενον περὶ πάτρης
Ἕκτορα·
sentences.tr:
hos de moi oios eēn, eiryto de asty kai autous,
ton sy prōiēn kteinas amynomenon peri patrēs
Hektora·
sentences.i: but the one who alone remained to me, who guarded the city and its people, him you killed only lately as he defended his native land: Hector;
sentences.n: ὃς δέ μοι οἶος ἔην is ‘but the one who was alone to me’, the only one still alive; εἴρυτο is ‘guarded’ (the imperfect of ἐρύομαι, with the epic initial εἰ-) and αὐτούς ‘themselves’ means the inhabitants. τὸν σὺ … κτεῖνας is ‘him you … having killed’, with πρῴην ‘a while ago’, and ἀμυνόμενον περὶ πάτρης is ‘defending himself for his native land’. Ἕκτορα is the object, delayed to the end of the sentence for effect.

sentences.t:
τοῦ νῦν εἵνεχ’ ἱκάνω νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
λυσόμενος παρὰ σεῖο, φέρω δ’ ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα.
sentences.tr:
tou nyn heinech’ hikanō nēas Achaiōn
lysomenos para seio, pherō d’ apereisi’ apoina.
sentences.l:
for his sake now I have come to the ships of the Achaeans
to ransom him from you, and I bring unstinted ransom.
sentences.i: For his sake I have now come to the ships of the Achaeans, to ransom him from you, and I bring an unstinted ransom.
sentences.n: τοῦ … εἵνεχ’ is ‘because of him’ (εἵνεκα, with the genitive that comes first). ἱκάνω is ‘I come’, a variant of ἱκνέομαι. λυσόμενος is the future participle of λύομαι ‘ransom’, giving purpose: ‘to ransom (him)’, and παρὰ σεῖο ‘from you’ (σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ). φέρω δ’ ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα is ‘and I bring unstinted ransom’, the same phrase as in the opening of the poem, but now in Priam’s mouth.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αἰδεῖο θεοὺς Ἀχιλεῦ, αὐτόν τ’ ἐλέησον
μνησάμενος σοῦ πατρός·
sentences.tr:
all’ aideio theous Achileu, auton t’ eleēson
mnēsamenos sou patros·
sentences.l:
But revere the gods, Achilles, and pity me myself,
remembering your father;
sentences.i: But revere the gods, Achilles, and pity me myself, remembering your father;
sentences.n: αἰδεῖο is the imperative of αἰδέομαι ‘revere’, with θεούς as object. ἐλέησον is the aorist imperative of ἐλεέω ‘pity’, and αὐτόν is ‘me myself’, because Priam is speaking of himself. μνησάμενος is the aorist participle ‘having remembered’, and σοῦ πατρός ‘your father’ closes the circle with line 486.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἐλεεινότερός περ,
ἔτλην δ’ οἷ’ οὔ πώ τις ἐπιχθόνιος βροτὸς ἄλλος,
sentences.tr:
egō d’ eleeinoteros per,
etlēn d’ hoi’ ou pō tis epichthonios brotos allos,
sentences.l:
and I am even more pitiable,
and I endured what no other mortal on earth yet has,
sentences.i: and I am even more pitiable, and I have endured what no other mortal on earth has yet endured,
sentences.n: ἐγὼ δ’ is ‘and I’. ἐλεεινότερος is the comparative ‘more pitiable’ (than Peleus), with περ ‘even’ for emphasis. ἔτλην is ‘I endured, bore to do’, the aorist of τλάω. οἷ’ is ‘such things as’; οὔ πώ τις … ἄλλος ‘no other yet’ and ἐπιχθόνιος βροτός ‘mortal upon the earth’. The thing endured is named in the next line.

sentences.t: ἀνδρὸς παιδοφόνοιο ποτὶ στόμα χεῖρ’ ὀρέγεσθαι.
sentences.tr: andros paidophonoio poti stoma cheir’ oregesthai.
sentences.l: to stretch to my mouth the hand of the man who killed my children.”
sentences.i: to reach to my mouth the hand of the man who killed my children.”
sentences.n: ὀρέγεσθαι is the middle infinitive of ὀρέγω ‘stretch out’, ‘to stretch out for myself’. ἀνδρὸς παιδοφόνοιο ‘of the child-slaying man’ goes with χεῖρ’ ‘hand’, and ποτὶ στόμα is ‘to the mouth’; the Greek does not say whose mouth, but the sense is Priam’s own, kissing Achilles’ hand as he did at 478. παιδοφόνοιο is ‘child-slaying’ (παῖς ‘child’ + root of φόνος). The closing mark ends Priam’s speech, Achilles’ reaction comes in the next part.
